chapters.title: Chapter 1: Fourth Amendment Protection of the Home and the Warrant Requirement
chapters.description: Introduces the central Fourth Amendment principles governing entries into and searches of a dwelling, the primacy of warrants, and recognized exceptions.
subtopics: Reasonableness and the sanctity of the home
The default warrant requirement for home entry
Curtilage and threshold concepts
Knock-and-talk doctrine and implied license to approach
Core exceptions overview: consent, exigent circumstances, plain view, protective sweep (Buie) basics
Limits on the community-caretaking doctrine after Caniglia v. Strom

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Landmark—Voluntary Consent to Search: Schneckloth and Bumper
chapters.description: Covers the constitutional doctrine that consent is a valid exception to the warrant requirement only if freely and voluntarily given, and explains what renders consent involuntary.
subtopics: Schneckloth v. Bustamonte: totality-of-the-circumstances test; knowledge of right to refuse not required
Bumper v. North Carolina: invalidity of consent obtained by claim of lawful authority (e.g., assertion of a warrant)
Indicators of voluntariness vs. mere acquiescence to authority
Government’s burden to prove voluntariness by a preponderance

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Voluntariness Factors and Consent Dynamics
chapters.description: Expands on how courts assess voluntariness in everyday policing contexts, focusing on tone, setting, and human factors.
subtopics: Common voluntariness factors: age, education, advisement of rights, detention length, repeated requests, custody, and coercion
Effect of time of day, number of officers, weapons display, and officer demeanor
Refusal followed by later consent; repeated requests and persistence
Verbal vs. nonverbal consent; opening a door or stepping aside
Ambiguous language and clarifying questions

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Landmark—Third-Party Consent: Matlock and Progeny
chapters.description: Explains when a co-occupant or spouse may authorize entry or a search, including limits when another resident objects.
subtopics: United States v. Matlock: common authority and joint access/control
Illinois v. Rodriguez: apparent authority and reasonable mistakes
Georgia v. Randolph: present and objecting co-occupant rule
Fernandez v. California: consent after lawful removal of an objecting occupant
Challenging third-party consent and expectation of privacy concepts

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Landmark—Scope of Consent: Florida v. Jimeno and Related Principles
chapters.description: Describes how courts determine what areas and actions are permitted by a given consent, using an objective reasonableness standard.
subtopics: Florida v. Jimeno: what a typical reasonable person would understand
Defining purpose, spatial limits, and duration of consent
Consent to enter vs. consent to search; movement within a home
Limiting, clarifying, and revoking consent
Containers, closed spaces, and implied scope

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Exigent Circumstances and the Emergency Aid Doctrine
chapters.description: Covers warrant exceptions permitting entry to prevent harm or address urgent threats, with attention to domestic-violence and welfare-check contexts.
subtopics: Emergency aid to protect persons vs. preventing evidence destruction
Domestic-violence and 911 call contexts supporting exigency
Objective, articulable facts and time sensitivity
Police-created exigency limits
Relationship to and distinction from community caretaking and protective sweeps

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Exclusionary Rule and Causation Doctrines
chapters.description: Explains suppression as a remedy and the exceptions that may admit evidence even after a Fourth Amendment violation.
subtopics: Fruit of the poisonous tree and proximate causation
Independent source (Murray) and inevitable discovery (Nix)
Attenuation doctrine
Good-faith exception (Leon, Herring, Davis) overview
Burden allocations and evidentiary showings for exceptions

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Federal Suppression Practice and Procedure
chapters.description: Outlines how suppression issues are litigated in federal court and the role of magistrate judges.
subtopics: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 12: motions to suppress and timing
Evidentiary hearings and the use of hearsay
Burden of production and persuasion
Magistrate judge reports and recommendations (28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)) and district court review
Preservation and waiver of arguments

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Conditional Guilty Pleas and Appellate Jurisdiction
chapters.description: Explains how a defendant may plead guilty while preserving the right to appeal suppression issues.
subtopics: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(a)(2) requirements
Scope of issues that can be reserved on appeal
Consequences of an unconditional plea
Appellate jurisdiction after a conditional plea

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Standards of Review on Appeal of Suppression Rulings
chapters.description: Details how appellate courts review district court suppression decisions, distinguishing factual from legal questions.
subtopics: Clear-error review for factual findings and voluntariness assessments
De novo review for legal conclusions and constitutional reasonableness
Mixed questions and circuit-specific approaches
Deference to credibility determinations

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Landmark—Video Evidence and Appellate Factfinding: Scott v. Harris
chapters.description: Addresses how clear video recordings can shape or control the factual narrative on appeal.
subtopics: When video evidence can override testimonial accounts
Applying the “blatantly contradicts” standard beyond summary judgment
Body-worn camera evidence and its limits
Interaction with clear-error review and deference

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Police-Citizen Encounters at the Doorway
chapters.description: Analyzes consent and coercion at home thresholds, where many Fourth Amendment disputes arise.
subtopics: Requesting entry vs. asserting authority
Threshold seizures and Mendenhall factors
Time, location, and tone as coercion indicators
Handling refusals, re-requests, and implied consent by conduct

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Warrants Based on Post-Entry Information
chapters.description: Explains how information obtained during an initial entry can support a subsequent warrant, and how taint is evaluated.
subtopics: Probable cause standards for search warrants
Use of witness statements (including minors) in affidavits
Independent source vs. derivative taint
Executing warrants and scope within a residence

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Federal Firearms Prohibition—18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)
chapters.description: Provides the substantive elements of the felon-in-possession offense relevant to understanding the charged crime.
subtopics: Elements of § 922(g)(1) and Rehaif’s knowledge requirement
Possession: actual and constructive
Interstate commerce nexus
Stipulations and proof at trial

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Applying Precedent and Multi-Factor Tests in Fourth Amendment Cases
chapters.description: Guides how courts synthesize case law and apply totality and objective-reasonableness standards to varied fact patterns.
subtopics: Using Supreme Court and circuit precedent to frame analysis
Weighing multi-factor voluntariness tests
Objective reasonableness for scope determinations
Distinguishing coercion from urgency and concern in police interactions
